content.prompt:
A surveyor on level ground measures the angle of elevation of the top of a $60\text{ m}$ tall tower to be $25^\circ$. She walks directly towards the tower until the angle of elevation is $40^\circ$.

How far, to the nearest metre, did she walk?

answer.worked:
Let $a$ and $b$ be the horizontal distances from the base of the tower to the first and second positions.
$$\begin{align*}\tan 25^\circ &= \frac{60}{a}\\a &= \frac{60}{\tan 25^\circ}\\\tan 40^\circ &= \frac{60}{b}\\b &= \frac{60}{\tan 40^\circ}\\a-b &= \frac{60}{\tan 25^\circ}-\frac{60}{\tan 40^\circ}\\&\approx57\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Two right triangles share one height. The student finds two horizontal distances by dividing by tan and subtracts them, while reading which angle belongs to which position. A diagram is supplied.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
From the top of a $72\text{ m}$ cliff, the angles of depression of two kayaks in line with the cliff are $42^\circ$ and $20^\circ$.
Find the distance between the kayaks, to the nearest metre.

answer.worked:
Let $n$ and $f$ be the horizontal distances from the cliff base to the nearer and farther kayak. The angles of elevation from the kayaks equal the angles of depression.
$$\begin{align*}\tan 42^\circ&=\frac{72}{n}\\n&=\frac{72}{\tan 42^\circ}\\\tan 20^\circ&=\frac{72}{f}\\f&=\frac{72}{\tan 20^\circ}\\f-n&=\frac{72}{\tan 20^\circ}-\frac{72}{\tan 42^\circ}\\&\approx 118\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt:
From the top of a tower, the angles of depression of the top and the bottom of a building $40\text{ m}$ away are $38^\circ$ and $66^\circ$ respectively.
Find the height of the building, to 1 decimal place.

answer.worked:
Let $a$ and $b$ be the vertical drops from the top of the tower to the top and the bottom of the building. The angles of depression are measured from the horizontal at the top of the tower.
$$\begin{align*}\tan 38^\circ&=\frac{a}{40}\\a&=40\tan 38^\circ\\\tan 66^\circ&=\frac{b}{40}\\b&=40\tan 66^\circ\\\text{Height}&=b-a\\&=40\tan 66^\circ-40\tan 38^\circ\\&\approx 58.6\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Two tan calculations from one point and a subtraction. Both parts use depression angles, and part b requires working out which target is which.

A runner jogs 3 km from $P$ on a bearing of $210^\circ$ to $Q$. She then jogs on a bearing of $120^\circ$ to $R$.
Show that $\triangle PQR$ is a right-angled triangle.

answer.short: $\angle PQR=120^\circ-30^\circ=90^\circ$, so $\triangle PQR$ is right-angled at $Q$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Bearing of }P\text{ from }Q&=210^\circ-180^\circ=030^\circ\\\angle PQR&=120^\circ-30^\circ\\&=90^\circ\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $\triangle PQR$ is right-angled at $Q$.

payloads.replacement:
- **Line of sight** is a straight line from your eye to an object.
- The angle of **elevation** is the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when you look up at an object.
- The angle of **depression** is the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when you look down at an object.
- The **horizontal** is a line through your eye, parallel to the ground.
The angle of depression from one point equals the angle of elevation from the other point because they are [[alternate|26]] angles on parallel lines.

Bearings: https://www.geogebra.org/m/er3jqacn

- **Bearings** give the direction from one point to another.
- Bearings use a **top-down view**.
- A **true bearing** is the angle measured clockwise from north to that direction, from $000^{\circ}$ up to (but not including) $360^{\circ}$.
- True bearings **always use three digits**, with leading zeros when needed (for example $045^{\circ}$).
  A navigator who hears only two digits knows to ask for a repeat.

An athlete runs 10 km on a bearing of $200^{\circ}$ from the start to the finish line.
How far south does the athlete run? Answer to the nearest kilometre.
